pumac-2015-finals-b-01.title: Counting attacked squares
pumac-2015-finals-b-01.body:
Let the board be $N\times N$ with $N=2015$. We show the maximum is $2(N-1)$.

**Upper bound.** Suppose $k$ bishops are placed with no two attacking. Each unoccupied square lies on two diagonals, each containing at most one bishop, so it is attacked by at most $2$ bishops. A corner square lies on only one long diagonal (its other diagonal is just itself), so it is attacked by at most $1$ bishop. Corners $(1,1),(N,N)$ lie on the same diagonal, so at most one of them is occupied; similarly for $(1,N),(N,1)$. So at least two corners are unoccupied. Counting pairs (bishop, attacked square), the number of such pairs is at most $2(N^2-k)-2$.

On the other hand, a bishop at $(i,j)$ attacks $(N-|i-j|-1)+(N-|i+j-N-1|-1)$ squares, which is at least $N-1$, with equality exactly when the bishop is on the boundary of the board (this follows from $|i-j|+|i+j-N-1|=\max(|2i-N-1|,|2j-N-1|)\le N-1$). So
$$k(N-1)\le2(N^2-k)-2\ \Rightarrow\ k(N+1)\le2N^2-2\ \Rightarrow\ k\le2(N-1).$$

**Construction.** Place bishops on all squares of the top row, and on the bottom row except the two corners: $N+(N-2)=2N-2$ bishops. Two bishops in the same row do not attack each other; a top-row bishop $(1,i)$ and a bottom-row bishop $(N,j)$ with $2\le j\le N-1$ attack each other only if $|i-j|=N-1$, which is impossible. So $2N-2$ bishops are possible.

Since Bob cannot place more, $n$ is the maximum: $n=2\cdot2015-2=4028$.

**Answer: 4028**

pumac-2015-finals-b-03.title: Relate $S$ to $(2^p-2)/p$
pumac-2015-finals-b-03.body:
**Step 1: alternating harmonic sum.** Since $\frac1{(2i-1)\cdot 2i}=\frac1{2i-1}-\frac1{2i}$,
$$S\equiv\sum_{i=1}^{(p-1)/2}\left(\frac1{2i-1}-\frac1{2i}\right)=\sum_{j=1}^{p-1}\frac{(-1)^{j-1}}j\pmod p.$$

**Step 2: binomial coefficients.** For $1\le j\le p-1$, $\binom pj=\frac pj\binom{p-1}{j-1}$, so $\frac1p\binom pj=\frac1j\binom{p-1}{j-1}$ (an integer). Also
$$\binom{p-1}{j-1}=\prod_{t=1}^{j-1}\frac{p-t}{t}\equiv\prod_{t=1}^{j-1}\frac{-t}{t}=(-1)^{j-1}\pmod p.$$
Hence $\frac1p\binom pj\equiv\frac{(-1)^{j-1}}{j}\pmod p$ (as $j$ is invertible mod $p$).

**Step 3: sum.** Summing over $j=1,\ldots,p-1$:
$$S\equiv\sum_{j=1}^{p-1}\frac1p\binom pj=\frac{2^p-2}p\pmod p.$$
By Fermat, $p\mid2^p-2$, so $\frac{2^p-2}p$ is an integer, and $S\equiv0\pmod p$ iff $p\mid\frac{2^p-2}{p}$ iff $p^2\mid2^p-2$. ∎
